overview: Meridian Energy is New Zealand's largest electricity generator and a major retailer, producing 100% renewable electricity from hydro (Waitaki and Manapōuri/Waiau schemes) and a growing wind and solar/battery fleet across both islands. It is a vertically integrated "gentailer": wholesale generation is paired with retail supply under the Meridian and Powershop NZ brands, plus a large fixed-price supply contract to the Tiwai Point aluminium smelter (NZAS/Rio Tinto). The company is 51% owned by the New Zealand Crown and also trades on the ASX (MEZ); FY ends 30 June.

business_model.summary: Meridian earns an 'energy margin' from generating renewable electricity (hydro, wind, growing solar) and selling it through three channels: retail customers (mass market + corporate/industrial, via Meridian and Powershop brands), wholesale/financial contract sales to other participants, and a large fixed-volume contract to the NZAS Tiwai Point smelter. Physical generation not used to meet contracted retail/wholesale/NZAS load is sold into the spot market, and shortfalls are bought from spot — this hedge book is the core of gentailer economics. H1 FY2026 energy margin was NZ$708m (up from $444m in H1 FY2025), EBITDAF $506m (up from $257m), largely a hydrology-driven swing (abundant inflows and low spot prices cut the cost of covering contracted sales).

revenue_streams.name: Generation sold at spot / to wholesale market

business_model.customer_type: Mix of B2C mass-market retail (residential, SMB, agricultural), B2B corporate & industrial, and one very large single industrial customer (NZAS aluminium smelter)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand generation and retail (hydro assets concentrated in South Island Waitaki/Manapōuri catchments; wind/solar spread across both islands); ASX-listed (MEZ) for capital-markets access only, no offshore operations

main_competitors: Independent retailers (Flick, Octopus NZ, Electric Kiwi)
competitive_position.market_position: Largest electricity generator in New Zealand by output and the largest renewable generator; one of the 'big four' vertically integrated gentailers that dominate NZ generation and retail; ~19.5% retail market share as of H1 FY2026 (up from 17.5% a year earlier, boosted by the August 2025 acquisition of ex-Flick customers)

moat_factors.description: Waitaki and Manapōuri hydro schemes have near-zero marginal cost and cannot be replicated (consents, catchment rights, decades-old capital); provides a cost advantage versus thermal and even most renewables
Largest gentailer allows netting of generation and retail load, reducing reliance on volatile spot market and smoothing hydrology risk versus a pure generator or pure retailer
Positions Meridian favourably with corporate and government customers seeking renewable PPAs and with green-bond investors (green finance framework used for latest debt issuance)
New hydro and large-scale generation face lengthy, costly, contestable consenting (e.g., Waitaki reconsenting, Pūkaki lake lowering fast-track) that limits new large-scale entrants
20-year contract to 2044 with demand-response optionality gives Meridian a very large, though price-capped, baseload customer and system flexibility revenue

weaknesses: Single-customer concentration risk: NZAS/Tiwai Point is a material share of Meridian's generation supply and system load; while the 2044 contract reduces near-term closure risk, the smelter remains a swing factor for South Island wholesale prices
Hydrology dependence makes reported earnings and cash flow highly volatile year to year, unlike a typical regulated utility
Heavy ongoing growth capex (wind/solar/battery pipeline) depresses free cash flow and requires continued debt funding
51% Crown ownership constrains capital structure/dividend flexibility and creates political risk (SOE-adjacent scrutiny, regulatory intervention)
Retail brand differentiation is limited; competition from independent, lower-cost retailers (Flick, Octopus) is intensifying, and asset-light entrants can undercut on price without owning generation

growth_drivers: Renewable build-out pipeline: Ruakākā solar (130MW/230GWh, $227m capex, first power Q4 2026), Te Rahui Stage 1 solar JV (200MW/384GWh, full power mid-2027), Mt Munro wind (85MW/360GWh, targeting FID Q4 2026), Te Rere Hau wind (170MW/750GWh, FID targeted Q4 2026) and a further ~15.3TWh of consented/consenting/prospective projects excluding completed construction
500MW/2,400GWh battery energy storage pipeline (including the completed 100MW/200MWh Ruakākā BESS) to firm intermittent wind/solar and capture price volatility
Structural NZ demand growth from electrification (EVs — 418 Zero public charge points installed; industrial/process heat conversion) and rising data-centre/AI load

Retail growth and cost-to-serve improvement from the Kraken platform migration (75k customers migrated as of Feb 2026; mass market migration targeted complete by June 2026, corporate & industrial by October 2026), enabling further market-share gains after the ex-Flick customer acquisition lifted share to 19.5%
Demand-response revenue from the NZAS contract's four-tier option structure, monetising system flexibility rather than just energy sales
Tight NZ electricity supply-demand balance (declining gas fields, retiring thermal capacity) supporting medium-term wholesale price levels once the current hydro-driven price trough passes

business.description: NZAS (~13% of NZ electricity demand) is supplied substantially from Meridian's Manapōuri station under a 20-year contract (signed May 2024, running to 31 December 2044) with tiered demand-response options; while this materially de-risks near-term closure versus the pre-2024 rolling-notice regime, any future Rio Tinto strategic review, aluminium price shock, or exercise of contractual off-ramps would remove a large, low-volatility revenue stream and flood the South Island market with cheap surplus power, depressing wholesale prices broadly

Earnings and cash flow swing sharply with South Island lake inflows/storage. H1 FY2026 saw the second-highest July-December hydro inflows on record (144% of average) and average generation prices of just ~$18/MWh in early 2026 versus $200/MWh in the 2024 dry-year spike — the mirror-image risk is another prolonged dry period forcing high-cost spot purchases to meet retail/NZAS/hedge obligations

Independent, asset-light retailers and rival gentailers compete aggressively on price; new non-discrimination obligations (from 1 July 2026) will force Meridian to offer hedge contracts to competitors on the same terms it uses internally, eroding a structural retail advantage

financial.risk: Rising net debt to fund the capex programme
financial.description: December 2025 net debt was $1,655m (net debt/EBITDAF 1.9x on a trailing-12-month basis), up 10% from June 2025; $350m of 6.5-year green bonds issued September 2025 and a new $1B syndicated facility in December 2025 show continued reliance on debt markets to fund the growth pipeline

Statutory NPAT is heavily distorted by unrealised fair-value changes on energy and treasury hedges (e.g., a $1,259m NPBT swing in FY2025 alone), making reported NPAT a poor guide to underlying performance and creating headline earnings volatility for investors focused on GAAP numbers

regulatory.risk: Electricity Authority / Commerce Commission Energy Competition Task Force intervention
regulatory.description: A 2025-2026 joint review of the 'big four' gentailer market structure has produced non-discrimination obligations (NDOs) requiring gentailers to offer hedge/risk-management contracts to competitors on effectively the same terms used internally, coming into force 1 July 2026 with implementation plans due 3 September 2026; while full structural separation was not mandated, the regulatory direction of travel is toward reduced gentailer advantages and continued scrutiny of wholesale market conduct

Majority government ownership brings political risk around pricing, dividend policy, and potential future ownership or structural changes, and heightens sensitivity to public/political pressure over 'excess' gentailer profits during high wholesale price periods

regulatory.risk: Consenting risk on the development pipeline
regulatory.description: Waitaki reconsenting decision (expected Q3 2026) is subject to a Forest & Bird appeal right to the High Court; Pūkaki lake lowering is proceeding via the Fast-track regime; multiple solar/wind projects remain at consent-application stage, so delays or refusals could push out the growth pipeline

macro.risk: Gas supply decline constraining thermal backstop
macro.description: Declining Pohokura/Maui-area gas field production and thermal plant reliability issues have historically driven price spikes (2024 dry-year average $200/MWh) when hydro storage is low; the August 2025 Huntly Strategic Energy Reserve provides a partial system-security backstop but gas scarcity remains a structural, not cyclical, issue
As a capital-intensive, dividend-paying, bond-proxy-like equity with rising net debt, Meridian's valuation and funding costs are sensitive to NZ interest rate moves

2025 was the first year of a five-year regulatory period seeing lines/transmission company revenue rise over 40% versus the prior period, pressuring retail margins and end-customer bills (a pass-through risk to political/regulatory pressure on retailers)

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ wholesale electricity market is tightening structurally (declining gas supply, thermal plant retirements/reliability issues) even as near-term prices sit at multi-year lows due to record hydro storage; medium-term outlook supported by electrification demand growth (EVs, industrial decarbonisation, data centres) and a wave of new wind/solar/battery investment across the sector
macro_factors.cyclicality: High short-term earnings cyclicality driven by hydrology (a 'weather cycle' more than an economic cycle) — dry years compress EBITDAF sharply, wet years boost it; underlying demand is relatively defensive (electricity is a necessity)
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high — capital-intensive generation build programme funded partly by debt, and equity often valued as a bond-proxy/dividend yield play, both sensitive to NZ interest rates
key_input_costs: Wholesale spot electricity (to cover contracted sales shortfalls)
Construction/EPC costs for wind, solar and battery projects
Gas price (indirect, via its effect on thermal-set spot prices)

recent_developments.event: H1 FY2026 interim results: record operating cash flow $336m (+$286m YoY) and record EBITDAF $506m (+97% YoY, +14% vs 1H FY24), driven by the second-highest July-December hydro inflows on record and record wind generation; underlying NPAT $143m vs -$5m in 1H FY25; interim dividend declared 6.40cps (up 4.1% YoY, 85% imputed)

Wholesale spot prices collapsed to a 2026 average of ~$18/MWh (vs $152/MWh in 2025 and $200/MWh in 2024) on near-full system hydro storage; Waitaki storage 119% of average at end-January 2026 with 177% of average snow storage entering the 2026 winter, a strong position heading into FY2026 second half
Electricity Authority announced the Huntly Strategic Energy Reserve to support system security and price stability following the 2024 dry-year price spike
Acquisition of ex-Flick Electric retail customers lifted Meridian's retail market share from 17.5% to 19.5% and drove record retail sales volumes
NZ Windfarms acquisition completed, added to operating cost and generation base from July 2025
Neal Barclay stepped down as CEO after seven years, succeeded by CFO Mike Roan effective 30 June 2025; Mandy Simpson now CFO
Ruakākā Battery Energy Storage System (100MW/200MWh) completed and commissioned

NZAS/Meridian agreed to bring the interim demand-response arrangement to an early end (NZAS ramping production from 16 June 2025), with Meridian's ability to call NZAS demand-response options under the new 2044 contract framework resuming from 12 April 2026
Meridian issued NZ$350m of 6.5-year unsecured green bonds; in December 2025 transitioned multiple bilateral bank facilities into a single $1B syndicated facility

Electricity Authority/Commerce Commission Energy Competition Task Force confirmed non-discrimination obligations (rather than full structural separation) as the preferred mechanism to level the playing field between gentailers and independent retailers/generators, coming into force 1 July 2026

guidance.fiscal_year: FY2026 (year ending 30 June 2026) — NOTE: FY2026 full-year results are scheduled for release 26 August 2026 and had NOT been published as of this analysis date (13 August 2026); figures below are guidance only, not actuals

items.notes: Unchanged from prior guidance; 2H FY26 includes continued Kraken platform implementation costs and the DigiGen programme
Unchanged from prior guidance; H1 FY26 capex was $86m ($53m growth incl. Ruakākā solar construction start, $33m stay-in-business); 2H FY26 expected to include higher spend on current projects

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Mike Roan and CFO Mandy Simpson highlighted a strong earnings reversion in 1H FY26 versus the dry-year-depressed 1H FY25, with momentum continuing through January 2026 despite very low (~$18/MWh) average generation prices. Management flagged high storage entering winter 2026 (Pūkaki near 100% full, 250GWh snow storage) as supportive, noted dual retail-system costs from the Kraken migration should cease in 2027, and said a delay to Te Rere Hau will see Mt Munro wind construction brought forward. No explicit FY2026 full-year EBITDAF or NPAT guidance figure was identified in the interim materials reviewed; management characterised the outlook as constructive given hydrology and demand trends, but did not commit to a numeric EBITDAF range.

bull_case: Irreplaceable, near-zero-marginal-cost renewable (hydro-led) asset base that cannot be replicated, giving Meridian structurally lower generation costs than thermal or newer-build competitors

Structural NZ electricity demand growth from electrification (EVs, industrial decarbonisation, data centres) against a tightening supply backdrop (gas field depletion, thermal retirements) supports medium-term wholesale price and margin durability once the current hydro-driven price trough normalises

The 2044 NZAS/Tiwai Point contract materially reduces the multi-decade closure/off-ramp overhang that dogged the stock for years, converting a binary risk into a structured, demand-response-optionality relationship

Large, funded renewable development pipeline (Ruakākā, Te Rahui, Mt Munro, Te Rere Hau, plus consenting/fast-track projects and a 500MW/2,400GWh battery pipeline) provides a multi-year growth runway in a capital-scarce, high-barrier-to-entry industry
Reliable, largely imputed dividend (interim 6.40cps, up 4.1% YoY) with a dividend reinvestment plan, appealing to income-focused NZ retail and institutional investors
bear_case: Heavy multi-year growth capex ($330m-$360m guided for FY2026 alone, with billions more in the pipeline) structurally depresses free cash flow and requires ongoing debt funding — net debt rose 10% in just six months to December 2025 — a key flag for any FCF-based DCF valuation, which should use normalized/mid-cycle rather than reported capex-heavy FCF

Hydrology volatility makes earnings genuinely unpredictable year to year (EBITDAF nearly doubled H1 FY26 vs H1 FY25 purely on inflow timing), making the stock behave more like a weather-driven cyclical than a stable utility despite trading on utility-like multiples

Regulatory direction of travel is unfavourable: new non-discrimination obligations effective 1 July 2026 will force Meridian to share hedge-contract terms with competitors on the same basis used internally, eroding the retail/wholesale integration advantage, with further Commerce Commission/Electricity Authority scrutiny an ongoing risk given the 2025-26 Energy Competition Task Force review

51% Crown ownership constrains strategic and capital flexibility and creates political risk, particularly around pricing and dividends during periods of high wholesale prices or public cost-of-living pressure

Despite the 2044 contract, NZAS/Tiwai Point remains a very large single counterparty; any future Rio Tinto strategic review, aluminium price collapse, or exercise of contractual mechanisms would still be a major shock to South Island wholesale prices and Meridian's earnings mix

As a high-multiple, bond-proxy-like equity with a large capex programme, Meridian is exposed to rising NZ interest rates both through funding costs and through valuation compression versus fixed income alternatives
